item.title: Child Care Pandemic Funds: HHS Can Help States Better Prepare for Future Emergencies and Ongoing Challenges
item.description:
What GAO Found
In GAO’s survey, states reported that useful strategies for spending Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF) pandemic funds included obtaining technical assistance from officials in the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and using partners such as local organizations to disburse funds.
While states spent more than 99 percent of pandemic child care funds, most reported that it was challenging to do so. States reported gaps in their readiness, such as inadequate technology to disburse a large influx of funds to child care providers. By encouraging states to assess their readiness to spend any new, temporary, or emergency CCDF funds that may be authorized in the future, HHS could help states more effectively disburse funding when those situations arise.
Nearly all states reported that increasing technical assistance for child care providers, auditing providers’ use of funds, and adding monitoring capacity to oversee funds and in some cases prevent fraud, were useful strategies for monitoring pandemic funds. However, over half of states reported specific monitoring challenges, such as ensuring that providers understood allowable uses of the funds. While most states reported that HHS guidance was useful, there were aspects of HHS guidance that several states and stakeholders reported as not useful. HHS has developed a plan for future emergencies, but it has not sought state administrators’ recent feedback on whether its planned approach sufficiently addresses the monitoring challenges states experienced with pandemic funds.
Several States and Stakeholders Reported Aspects of HHS Guidance That Could Have Been Improved So States Could Better Monitor Funds
Nearly all states reported on the survey that since pandemic funding expired, at least one of the outcomes they achieved with pandemic funds, such as serving more families with subsidies, had ended. Moving forward, all states said that they anticipated CCDF program challenges in fiscal year 2026 and most said that additional guidance from HHS could help address these challenges. States’ most frequently expected challenges included the affordability of child care, availability of quality care, and maintaining the financial stability of providers in the state.
HHS officials told GAO that they are helping states with affordability and availability by rescinding certain regulations. HHS officials said they had also updated a business skills training for providers but had not provided additional resources to states on helping providers address rising costs since the pandemic. State officials and stakeholders GAO spoke with said that, in light of rising costs, providers could benefit from more assistance managing their businesses. By providing more support to states to help providers, HHS could better ensure that families have stable access to child care.
Why GAO Did This Study
During the COVID-19 pandemic, Congress appropriated $52.5 billion in supplemental funding for CCDF to stabilize the child care sector. GAO was asked to report on states’ use and HHS’s oversight of these funds.This report examines: (1) strategies states found useful in spending pandemic funds and challenges they encountered, (2) strategies states found useful in monitoring these funds, challenges they encountered, and the extent to which they view HHS oversight as sufficient, and (3) the extent to which states are sustaining key outcomes of this funding, and the extent to which they need HHS support on current challenges. This report follows previous GAO reports on pandemic child care funding (GAO-22-105051 and GAO-24-106258).
GAO reviewed relevant federal laws, regulations, and HHS guidance to states. From January to March 2026, GAO surveyed child care administrators in 49 states. GAO also interviewed officials in four states selected for factors such as amount of pandemic funds received, seven providers across the selected states, 19 stakeholders with expertise in child care and pandemic funding, and HHS officials.
